classification.difficultyReason: Connect two SAS congruence proofs to equal radii, then use SSS and a straight angle to establish the third perpendicular bisector and conclude uniqueness.

inlines.text: The circle passing through all three vertices of a triangle is called a
The following theorem not only shows that every triangle has a unique circumcircle, but also shows how to construct the circumcircle.
The three perpendicular bisectors of a triangle are concurrent. Their point of intersection (called the circumcentre) is the centre of a circle (called a circumcircle).
Prove this theorem using congruence. In the diagram, the midpoints of

spec.description: Triangle ABC with midpoint ticks in three distinct groups, perpendicular segments OR and OQ marked by right-angle squares, and OP unmarked at P. Red dashed OA, OB and OC distinguish the proposed radii. Ordinary source-blue geometry is black in house style.
spec.mathematics: P, Q and R bisect BC, CA and AB respectively; OR is perpendicular to AB and OQ is perpendicular to CA. Perpendicularity of OP to BC is to be proved.

answer.short:
$OA=OB=OC$ by SAS congruence at $R$ and $Q$. SSS congruence gives $\angle BPO=\angle CPO=90^\circ$, so the third perpendicular bisector also passes through $O$.

The circle with centre $O$ and radius $OA$ passes through all three vertices; its centre is uniquely determined by the perpendicular bisectors.
answer.worked:
Let the perpendicular bisectors of $AB$ and $AC$ meet at $O$.

In $\triangle ARO$ and $\triangle BRO$:
$$\begin{align*}AR&=BR &&\text{(midpoint)}\\\angle ARO&=\angle BRO=90^\circ &&\text{(perpendicular bisector)}\\OR&=OR &&\text{(common)}\end{align*}$$
Thus $\triangle ARO\equiv\triangle BRO$ (SAS), so $OA=OB$ (matching sides).

In $\triangle AQO$ and $\triangle CQO$:
$$\begin{align*}AQ&=CQ &&\text{(midpoint)}\\\angle AQO&=\angle CQO=90^\circ &&\text{(perpendicular bisector)}\\OQ&=OQ &&\text{(common)}\end{align*}$$
Thus $\triangle AQO\equiv\triangle CQO$ (SAS), so $OA=OC$ (matching sides). Hence $OA=OB=OC$.

In $\triangle BPO$ and $\triangle CPO$:
$$\begin{align*}BP&=CP &&\text{(midpoint)}\\OB&=OC &&\text{(proved above)}\\OP&=OP &&\text{(common)}\end{align*}$$
Thus $\triangle BPO\equiv\triangle CPO$ (SSS), so $\angle BPO=\angle CPO$ (matching angles). These adjacent angles form a straight angle, so each is $90^\circ$. Therefore $OP\perp BC$.

All three perpendicular bisectors pass through $O$, so they are concurrent. Since $OA=OB=OC$, the circle with centre $O$ and radius $OA$ passes through $A$, $B$ and $C$.

Any circumcentre must lie on the perpendicular bisectors of $AB$ and $AC$, which have only one intersection. Therefore the circumcentre, and hence the circumcircle, is unique.
